title: Capturing certificates from servers
summary: Pull the certificate chain off a live server with openssl s_client, curl, PowerShell, nmap and a browser, and read what came back.

**Why `-servername`?** One IP address often hosts many sites. The client names the site it wants in the TLS ClientHello (SNI) and the server picks the matching certificate. Without SNI you get the **default** certificate, which is often for a different site. Recent OpenSSL sends SNI from the `-connect` host automatically, but you still need `-servername` when you connect to an IP address, a load balancer name or `localhost`.
On Windows PowerShell, use `$null |` instead of `</dev/null`.

steps.prompt: Here is part of the `s_client -showcerts` output. How many certificates did the server send?
code: verify error:num=19:self-signed certificate in certificate chain
Verify return code: 19 (self-signed certificate in certificate chain)
steps.explain: Entries 0, 1 and 2: leaf, intermediate and root (`s:` subject, `i:` issuer). Error 19 means the root is not in openssl's trust store, often a company's private CA. Sending the root is harmless but unnecessary.

steps.prompt: `openssl s_client -connect 203.0.113.10:443 -showcerts` returns `CN=default.hosting.example`, but browsers show a valid `shop.example` certificate. What happened?
options: Connecting to an IP sends no SNI, so the server returned its default certificate; add `-servername shop.example`
steps.explain: Always pass `-servername` with the real host name when you capture a certificate, or you may diagnose the wrong one.

steps.title: curl, PowerShell, nmap, browsers and Wireshark
body: curl -vI https://shop.example 2>&1 | grep -A8 "Server certificate"   # subject, dates, issuer, verify result
curl --cacert dojo-root.pem https://shop.example                     # trust one extra root, for this call
curl -k https://shop.example        # = --insecure: NO verification. Never in scripts or production
nmap --script ssl-cert -p 443 shop.example                           # subject, SAN, issuer, validity

PowerShell has no `-showcerts`. `Invoke-WebRequest` only tells you *that* validation failed (`The remote certificate is invalid according to the validation procedure`), so capture the certificate with `SslStream`:
The callback returns `$true` so you can **look at** a broken certificate. That's fine for a capture script that sends no data, and never fine in an app.
**Browsers:** padlock → certificate → Details → Export (Chrome/Edge: Base64 .crt or a chain .p7b; Firefox: "PEM (chain)").

**Wireshark:** in TLS 1.2 the `Certificate` handshake message is plain text, so you can export it. In **TLS 1.3** everything after ServerHello is encrypted: you see the SNI in the ClientHello, but not the certificate.

steps.prompt: Safe to use, or does it switch verification off?
steps.explain: Every 'disables' item turns a TLS connection into an unauthenticated one: anyone in the middle can impersonate the server. Fix trust instead (`--cacert`, a trust store, `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS`).

steps.prompt: The tests turn a chain into fake `s_client -showcerts` text and read it back. What does this print?
code: var root = DojoCert("CN=Shop Root CA", null, true, naYear: 2040);
var inter = DojoCert("CN=Shop Issuing CA", root, true);

+ " 1 s:CN = Shop Issuing CA
" + inter.ExportCertificatePem() + "
---
Verify return code: 0 (ok)
";
static X509Certificate2 DojoCert(string subject, X509Certificate2? issuer, bool isCa, string? dns = null, string? eku = null, int nbYear = 2030, int naYear = 2035)
var req = new CertificateRequest(subject, key, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256);
req.CertificateExtensions.Add(new X509KeyUsageExtension(isCa ? X509KeyUsageFlags.KeyCertSign | X509KeyUsageFlags.CrlSign : X509KeyUsageFlags.DigitalSignature, true));
if (dns != null) { var b = new SubjectAlternativeNameBuilder(); foreach (var d in dns.Split(',')) b.AddDnsName(d); req.CertificateExtensions.Add(b.Build()); }
if (eku != null) req.CertificateExtensions.Add(new X509EnhancedKeyUsageExtension(new OidCollection { new Oid(eku) }, false));
using var pub = req.Create(issuer, nb, na, serial);
answer: CN=Shop Issuing CA <- CN=Shop Root CA
steps.explain: `ImportFromPem` skips the text between PEM blocks, so you can feed it a raw `s_client` capture.

steps.title: Read a captured chain
prompt: Write `List<string> ChainFromTranscript(string transcript)`. It receives the text of an `openssl s_client -showcerts` run (noise, then PEM blocks) and returns one line per certificate **in the order the server sent them**, in openssl's own format:
1 s:CN=Shop Issuing CA i:CN=Shop Root CA
Then a final line saying whether the chain is in the right order: `order: ok` if each certificate's issuer is the next one's subject, otherwise `order: wrong`. (A single certificate is `order: ok`.)
template: var root = DojoCert("CN=Shop Root CA", null, true, naYear: 2040);
var inter = DojoCert("CN=Shop Issuing CA", root, true);

string DojoT(params X509Certificate2[] cs) => "CONNECTED(00000003)
depth=0 CN = x
---
Certificate chain
"
Dojo.Eq("leaf and intermediate", new List<string> { "0 s:CN=shop.example i:CN=Shop Issuing CA", "1 s:CN=Shop Issuing CA i:CN=Shop Root CA", "order: ok" }, ChainFromTranscript(DojoT(leaf, inter)));

Dojo.Eq("full chain with root", new List<string> { "0 s:CN=shop.example i:CN=Shop Issuing CA", "1 s:CN=Shop Issuing CA i:CN=Shop Root CA", "2 s:CN=Shop Root CA i:CN=Shop Root CA", "order: ok" }, ChainFromTranscript(DojoT(leaf, inter, root)));

Dojo.Eq("intermediate first is the wrong order", new List<string> { "0 s:CN=Shop Issuing CA i:CN=Shop Root CA", "1 s:CN=shop.example i:CN=Shop Issuing CA", "order: wrong" }, ChainFromTranscript(DojoT(inter, leaf)));
Dojo.Eq("leaf only", new List<string> { "0 s:CN=shop.example i:CN=Shop Issuing CA", "order: ok" }, ChainFromTranscript(DojoT(leaf)));
static X509Certificate2 DojoCert(string subject, X509Certificate2? issuer, bool isCa, string? dns = null, string? eku = null, int nbYear = 2030, int naYear = 2035)
var req = new CertificateRequest(subject, key, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256);
req.CertificateExtensions.Add(new X509KeyUsageExtension(isCa ? X509KeyUsageFlags.KeyCertSign | X509KeyUsageFlags.CrlSign : X509KeyUsageFlags.DigitalSignature, true));
if (dns != null) { var b = new SubjectAlternativeNameBuilder(); foreach (var d in dns.Split(',')) b.AddDnsName(d); req.CertificateExtensions.Add(b.Build()); }
if (eku != null) req.CertificateExtensions.Add(new X509EnhancedKeyUsageExtension(new OidCollection { new Oid(eku) }, false));
using var pub = req.Create(issuer, nb, na, serial);

steps.title: A safe alternative to -k: pin what you captured
prompt: `-k` accepts any certificate. When you must talk to a server with a private or self-signed certificate and cannot install its root, **pin** it instead: accept it only if its SHA-256 fingerprint matches the one you captured and checked.
Write the body of a validation callback: `bool Accept(X509Certificate2 cert, SslPolicyErrors errors, string pinnedSha256)`.
- exactly `RemoteCertificateChainErrors` (an unknown root) and the certificate's SHA-256 hex matches `pinnedSha256` (compare case-insensitively, ignoring `:`): accept
- anything else, **including a name mismatch**, even with the right pin: reject
starter: bool Accept(X509Certificate2 cert, SslPolicyErrors errors, string pinnedSha256)
solution: bool Accept(X509Certificate2 cert, SslPolicyErrors errors, string pinnedSha256)
template: Dojo.Eq("trusted normally: accept", true, Accept(dojoOther, SslPolicyErrors.None, dojoPin));
Dojo.Eq("unknown root, pin matches: accept", true, Accept(dojoCert, SslPolicyErrors.RemoteCertificateChainErrors, dojoPin));
Dojo.Eq("unknown root, different certificate: reject", false, Accept(dojoOther, SslPolicyErrors.RemoteCertificateChainErrors, dojoPin));
Dojo.Eq("name mismatch with the right pin: reject", false, Accept(dojoCert, SslPolicyErrors.RemoteCertificateNameMismatch, dojoPin));
Dojo.Eq("chain and name errors together: reject", false, Accept(dojoCert, SslPolicyErrors.RemoteCertificateChainErrors | SslPolicyErrors.RemoteCertificateNameMismatch, dojoPin));
static X509Certificate2 DojoCert(string subject, X509Certificate2? issuer, bool isCa, string? dns = null, string? eku = null, int nbYear = 2030, int naYear = 2035)
var req = new CertificateRequest(subject, key, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256);
req.CertificateExtensions.Add(new X509KeyUsageExtension(isCa ? X509KeyUsageFlags.KeyCertSign | X509KeyUsageFlags.CrlSign : X509KeyUsageFlags.DigitalSignature, true));
if (dns != null) { var b = new SubjectAlternativeNameBuilder(); foreach (var d in dns.Split(',')) b.AddDnsName(d); req.CertificateExtensions.Add(b.Build()); }
if (eku != null) req.CertificateExtensions.Add(new X509EnhancedKeyUsageExtension(new OidCollection { new Oid(eku) }, false));
using var pub = req.Create(issuer, nb, na, serial);
